column1: What is the peak age of incidence for intussusception in pediatric patients?
column2: 3 to 12 months

column1: Which preceding infection frequently triggers intussusception by causing Peyer's patch hypertrophy?
column2: Viral adenoviral illness

column1: What is the gold-standard initial imaging modality for diagnosing pediatric intussusception?
column2: Abdominal Ultrasound

column1: What classic sign is seen on transverse abdominal ultrasound in a patient with intussusception?
column2: "Target" sign (or "Donut" sign)

column1: What classic sign is seen on longitudinal abdominal ultrasound in intussusception?
column2: "Pseudokidney" sign

column1: What is the first-line non-operative definitive treatment for intussusception in the absence of peritonitis or shock?
column2: Pneumatic (air) or hydrostatic contrast reduction under fluoroscopic or ultrasound guidance

column1: What radiological finding on a contrast barium enema indicates an intussusception causing intestinal obstruction?
column2: "Claw sign" (or cup-shaped filling defect / meniscus sign)

column1: What is the most common anatomical form of intussusception in infants?
column2: Ileocolic intussusception

column1: What is the approximate success rate of pneumatic or hydrostatic reduction for intussusception?
Which clinical findings strictly contraindicate non-operative pneumatic reduction for intussusception?
column2: Peritonitis, shock, or evidence of intestinal perforation

column1: Clinical photo of a newborn baby with a visibly distended and discolored abdomen What serious neonatal intestinal emergency is characterized by bowel wall ischemia, distended abdomen, and rapid deterioration as shown above?
column2: Necrotizing Enterocolitis (NEC)

column1: Which infant population is predominantly affected by Necrotizing Enterocolitis (NEC)?
column2: Preterm infants in the first weeks of life

column1: What three primary factors contribute to the etiology of Necrotizing Enterocolitis?
column2: Ischemia of the bowel wall, infecting organisms, and milk feeding

column1: What are the immediate initial treatment steps when Necrotizing Enterocolitis is suspected in a neonate?
column2: Stop oral feeding (NPO) and administer IV broad-spectrum antibiotics

column1: What clinical features characterize Bell's Stage I (Suspected) Necrotizing Enterocolitis?
column2: Abdominal distension, gastric residuals (aspirated milk), lethargy, and normal or ileus X-ray

column1: What pathognomonic radiological sign confirms Bell's Stage II (Definite) Necrotizing Enterocolitis?
column2: Pneumatosis intestinalis (and/or portal venous gas)

column1: Which systemic laboratory abnormalities typically appear in Bell's Stage II Necrotizing Enterocolitis?
column2: Metabolic acidosis and thrombocytopenia

column1: What radiological finding defines Bell's Stage III (Advanced/Perforated) Necrotizing Enterocolitis?
column2: Pneumoperitoneum

column1: Name two classic abdominal X-ray signs that indicate pneumoperitoneum in advanced pediatric NEC.
column2: Rigler's sign and the Football sign

column1: What intervention is required for Bell's Stage III Necrotizing Enterocolitis?
column2: Emergency surgical laparotomy

column1: What is the most common surgical condition in infancy?
column2: Inguinal hernia

column1: How does an pediatric inguinal hernia typically present clinically?
column2: As an intermittent swelling in the inguinal region or scrotum noticed during crying or straining

column1: Why should surgical repair of an pediatric inguinal hernia be performed as soon as possible after diagnosis?
column2: To prevent the high risk of incarceration and strangulation

column1: List two differential diagnoses for acute abdominal pain in infants and toddlers.
column2: Intussusception and strangulated inguinal hernia (or acute appendicitis, midgut volvulus)

column1: In a child presenting with bilious vomiting, distension, and severe pain, what are two major surgical complications of untreated intestinal inflammation or infection?
column2: Peritonitis and intestinal perforation

column1: Which diagnostic blood tests assist in identifying enteric fever in a pediatric abdominal presentation?
column2: Full blood count (CP), Widal test, and blood culture

column1: What pressure profile is characteristically observed on cardiac catheterization in Tetralogy of Fallot?
column2: Right ventricular systolic pressure is equal to LV pressure, while pulmonary artery pressure is markedly reduced.

column1: What determines systemic arterial oxygen saturation in Tetralogy of Fallot?
column2: The magnitude of the right-to-left intra-cardiac shunt

column1: What non-pharmacological physical maneuver is the immediate first step when managing a hypercyanotic spell in an infant?
column2: Calming the infant and placing them on their abdomen in the knee-chest position

column1: What concentration of oxygen should be administered during an acute hypercyanotic spell?
column2: 100% oxygen via mask

column1: What intravenous medication is administered to manage an acute hypercyanotic spell in Tetralogy of Fallot?
column2: IV Propranolol ($0.1\text{--}0.2\text{ mg/kg}$)

column1: What oral maintenance dosage of propranolol is used for prophylaxis against hypercyanotic spells?
column2: $0.5\text{--}1\text{ mg/kg/dose}$ 2 to 3 times daily

column1: What is the initial management strategy for an asymptomatic Patent Ductus Arteriosus (PDA) in a preterm infant?
column2: Conservative observation to wait for spontaneous ductal closure

column1: Which intravenous medication is indicated for pharmacologic closure of a symptomatic Patent Ductus Arteriosus in a preterm infant?
column2: IV Indomethacin ($0.1\text{ mg/kg/day}$ for 3 doses)

column1: What is the recommended surgical timing for repair of a Patent Ductus Arteriosus (PDA)?
column2: As soon as diagnosis is established, preferably before 1 year of age

column1: What standard surgical procedure is performed to correct a Patent Ductus Arteriosus?
column2: Surgical ligation and division of the ductus via a left thoracotomy

column1: Which clinical presentation in a child requires urgent dilated indirect ophthalmoscopy under general anesthesia?
column2: Leukocoria (white pupillary reflex), new-onset strabismus, or abnormal red reflex

column1: Why is Fine Needle Aspiration Biopsy (FNAB) strictly contraindicated in suspected retinoblastoma?
column2: It poses a high risk of extraocular tumor seeding along the needle tract.

column1: Within what timeframe should urgent examination under anesthesia be conducted for suspected retinoblastoma?
column2: Within 1 to 2 weeks

column1: What immunopathologic abnormality defines Henoch-Schönlein Purpura (IgA Vasculitis)?
column2: Deposition of IgA1-containing immune complexes in small blood vessels

column1: How does the platelet count distinguish Henoch-Schönlein Purpura from idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP)?
column2: Platelet count is normal or elevated in HSP, whereas it is severely reduced in ITP.

column1: What organ involvement determines the long-term prognosis in Henoch-Schönlein Purpura?
column2: Severity of renal involvement (IgA nephritis)

column1: What serial monitoring routine is required for a child diagnosed with HSP?
column2: Serial urinalysis and blood pressure measurements for at least 6 to 12 months

column1: How is Late-Onset Neonatal Sepsis (LOS) defined temporally?
column2: Sepsis presenting after 72 hours of life

column1: What is the predominant bacterial organism causing Late-Onset Neonatal Sepsis?
column2: Coagulase-Negative Staphylococci (*Staphylococcus epidermidis*)

column1: Name three pathogens besides CoNS implicated in Late-Onset Neonatal Sepsis.
column2: *Staphylococcus aureus*, Gram-negative enteric bacilli (*E. coli*, *Klebsiella*), and Group B *Streptococcus*

column1: What duration defines an acute pediatric fever in clinical history taking?
column2: Fever lasting less than 7 days

column1: What fever pattern is classic for pediatric Dengue infection?
column2: High continuous fever

column1: List three clinical warning signs in a pediatric patient with suspected Dengue.
column2: Reduced feeding, bleeding manifestations, and severe abdominal pain / persistent vomiting

column1: On which specific day of the Dengue disease course must warning signs be monitored most closely?
column2: On the day of defervescence (when fever subsides)

column1: What is the clinical purpose of performing the Hess test (tourniquet test) in fever evaluation?
column2: To evaluate capillary fragility and assess likelihood of Dengue infection

column1: What count of petechiae per square inch was traditionally required to consider a Hess test positive?
column2: $>20$ petechiae per square inch ($\ge 10$ is now also considered positive)

column1: What are the pooled sensitivity and specificity of the Hess test for diagnosing Dengue?
column2: Sensitivity of 58% and specificity of 71%

column1: During which phase of illness does the Dengue NS1 Ag test yield its highest positivity rate?
column2: During the first 2 days of fever

column1: Which laboratory parameter must be checked before fluid resuscitation in a Group B2 Dengue patient?
column2: Hematocrit (Hct) / Complete Blood Count (CBC)
